items.title: Level 1: The five Success Profiles elements
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: The Civil Service uses a framework called Success Profiles to describe what a job needs and to decide who should get it. It is published on GOV.UK and is used for jobs at every grade, including Administrative Officer. Success Profiles has five elements. Behaviours are the actions and activities a person carries out that show how they work. Strengths are the things a person does well, does often and enjoys. Ability is the aptitude or potential to do a job, and it is often checked with tests. Experience is the knowledge and background gained in earlier activities, whether paid or unpaid. Technical is the specific professional skills or qualifications a job needs, such as an accountancy qualification. Not every job uses all five elements. The job advert on Civil Service Jobs says which ones will be assessed, so a job at the entry grades may use only a few of the five. Learning the five names is the first step in preparing, because the advert and the interview questions are built from them. The framework describes the job first and then looks for people who match it. Once you know the five names, you can read any advert and see at once what is going to be tested.

questions.hint: The advert on Civil Service Jobs lists the elements assessed for that role.

questions.hint: Technical means the specific professional skills or qualifications for the role.

questions.prompt: Which element is the aptitude or potential to do a job?
questions.hint: Ability is the aptitude or potential to do the job, often checked with tests.

questions.hint: Experience covers what you have learned from earlier activities, paid or unpaid.

items.title: Level 1: How many Behaviours and where to find them
items.body: The Civil Service Behaviours are a list of nine things that people do at work that lead to success. They are published on GOV.UK. The nine Behaviours are Seeing the Big Picture, Changing and Improving, Making Effective Decisions, Leadership, Communicating and Influencing, Working Together, Developing Self and Others, Managing a Quality Service and Delivering at Pace. Each Behaviour is described at several levels, from the entry grades up to the Senior Civil Service. A job advert tells you which Behaviours are tested for the role and at what level. An Administrative Officer role is at one of the lowest levels, so the descriptions are about everyday matters such as listening, being clear, helping colleagues and meeting deadlines. For a typical entry-level job the advert might ask for only a few of the nine, not the whole list. The usual way to prepare is to read the Behaviours named in your advert, read their descriptions for your level, and then think of two or three real examples from your own life for each one. Your examples can come from paid work, volunteering, study or home life. Keep a short written note of each example so that you can use it in an application form or an interview.

items.title: Level 1: Seeing the Big Picture and Changing and Improving
items.body: Two of the nine Civil Service Behaviours are Seeing the Big Picture and Changing and Improving. Seeing the Big Picture means understanding how your own work fits into the aims of your team, your department and the public it serves. At entry level it can be as simple as knowing why a form you process matters to the person who sent it. Changing and Improving means being open to new ways of working and suggesting ideas that make things better. At entry level it includes noticing when a task could be done more simply and telling your manager, as well as being willing to try a new system when one is introduced. Both Behaviours are about looking beyond the single task in front of you. A short example of Seeing the Big Picture could be a person who understands that answering letters accurately helps people get the benefit they are owed. A short example of Changing and Improving could be a person who suggests a clearer layout for a shared spreadsheet and then helps colleagues use it. In an application you would describe what you did, not just what you believe. Use real situations from work, volunteering or home. Remember that an advert may ask for just one of these two, or for neither, so always check which Behaviours are listed.

items.title: Level 1: Making Effective Decisions and Leadership
items.body: Making Effective Decisions and Leadership are two more of the nine Civil Service Behaviours. Making Effective Decisions means using information to reach sensible choices. At entry level it includes checking the facts, thinking about the options, asking for advice when you need it and being able to explain why you chose what you did. Leadership does not only mean being in charge. At entry level it is about being positive, treating people with respect, being helpful and showing others a good example, even when you have no staff to manage. People can show Leadership by supporting a new colleague, speaking up politely when something is wrong, or taking the lead on a small task. A short example of Making Effective Decisions could be someone who compares two quotes for a household repair and picks the one with the better value. A short example of Leadership could be a volunteer who welcomes new helpers and shows them what to do. Both Behaviours can be shown from any part of your life. When you write about them, say what you did and why, rather than only describing the situation. Remember that Leadership at entry level is about example and attitude, not about having a job title. Check your advert to see whether either of them is tested.

items.title: Level 1: Communicating and Influencing and Working Together
items.body: Communicating and Influencing and Working Together are two of the nine Civil Service Behaviours. Communicating and Influencing means getting your message across clearly, in speech and in writing, and listening to others. At entry level it includes writing clear emails, speaking politely on the phone, checking that people have understood, and choosing the right words for the person in front of you. Influencing means persuading others in a respectful way, for example by explaining your reasons. Working Together means building good working relationships and helping a team reach its goals. At entry level it includes sharing information, supporting colleagues who are busy, respecting different views and backgrounds, and doing your share of the work. Both Behaviours involve other people, but they are different. Communicating and Influencing is about the message and how you share it, while Working Together is about collaboration and teamwork. A short example of Communicating and Influencing could be someone who writes a clear notice for a community hall. A short example of Working Together could be someone who covers a shift for a colleague and then asks for help in return. When you describe your own examples, use the word I and give the result. Check your advert to see which of the nine are listed.

questions.hint: A clear written notice shows communication.

questions.hint: Mutual support shows Working Together.

items.title: Level 1: Developing Self and Others, Quality Service and Pace
items.body: Three more Civil Service Behaviours are Developing Self and Others, Managing a Quality Service and Delivering at Pace. Developing Self and Others means taking responsibility for your own learning, asking for feedback, and helping other people to learn. At entry level it includes going on training, learning from mistakes and showing a colleague how to do something. Managing a Quality Service means giving customers accurate and reliable service. At entry level it includes following procedures, checking your work for errors, keeping good records and treating each customer with courtesy. Delivering at Pace means getting the work done on time and doing it well. At entry level it includes planning your tasks, putting the most urgent first, keeping going when the work is busy and taking responsibility for meeting deadlines. Together these three Behaviours describe a reliable worker who learns, is accurate and is on time. A short example of Developing Self and Others could be someone who completes an evening course in basic IT. A short example of Managing a Quality Service could be a person who checks each form for missing details before sending it. A short example of Delivering at Pace could be a person who works through a long list of tasks in order of importance before a deadline.

items.title: Level 1: Strengths explained
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Strengths are one of the five Success Profiles elements. A strength is something you do well, do regularly and enjoy, and it usually gives you energy. This is different from a skill you have learned but find tiring. Strengths are assessed because people who enjoy the work they do tend to do it well and stay motivated. Strengths questions are often asked at interview. They tend to be short and quick, and you are asked to answer naturally. A typical strengths question might be 'What do you enjoy most about helping people?' or 'Would you prefer to work on one task at a time or many?' There is no single right answer, and interviewers listen to how you talk about the subject, not only to the words. Because the questions are quick, it is not helpful to memorise a script. Instead, prepare by thinking about what you are good at and what you enjoy in work, at home or in a hobby. Be honest, because the questions are designed to reveal what really gives you energy. Behaviours, by contrast, are usually answered with a past example, often prepared using the STAR method. Strengths-based questions do not usually need one. Your advert will say whether strengths are tested for the role.

items.title: Level 1: Ability and Technical explained
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Ability and Technical are two more elements of Success Profiles. Ability means the aptitude or potential to do a job. It is the natural capacity to learn and to do tasks such as reading information, working with numbers or making sound judgements. Ability is often measured with online tests, such as a verbal reasoning test, a numerical reasoning test or a judgement test. Many entry-level Civil Service jobs begin the application with such tests. You do not need a qualification to pass them, but practising helps because you learn the format and the timing. Technical means the specific professional skills or qualifications a job needs. Examples include a qualification in accountancy, a licence to drive a particular vehicle, or knowledge of a computer system. Technical requirements are listed in the job advert. Many Administrative Officer roles do not need a Technical element at all, because no formal qualification is required. When a job does need one, the advert says so clearly and says whether it must be held at the time of applying. Remember the difference: Ability is the potential to learn and perform, while Technical is the specific knowledge or qualification already needed. Read the advert for both before you apply.

items.title: Level 1: Experience in Success Profiles
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Experience is one of the five Success Profiles elements. It means the knowledge and background you have gained in previous activities. The activities can be paid or unpaid. This means a job, a work placement, volunteering, caring for family, running a household or helping at a community group can all count. The Civil Service wants to know what you have done and what you have learned from it. Experience questions on an application form often ask you to show how you have done something similar to what the job needs. For an Administrative Officer role this could be working with records, dealing with the public, using a computer, handling money or following a procedure. You do not need previous Civil Service experience. When you describe your experience, say what you did, how you did it and what the outcome was. Use plain, specific language and give details such as numbers, dates or the people you worked with. Do not apologise for unpaid or home experience. Describe it as work, because organising and caring involve real skills. Experience is also tested through follow-up questions at interview, so everything you write should be true and something you can explain. The advert says whether Experience is assessed.

items.title: Level 1: The four letters of STAR
items.body: STAR is a simple way to structure an example when you answer a Behaviours question. It is used in application forms and interviews for Civil Service jobs. The four letters stand for Situation, Task, Action and Result. Situation means setting the scene briefly: where you were, when it was and what was happening. Task means saying what you were responsible for or trying to achieve. Action means describing what you personally did, step by step. Result means saying what happened because of what you did, and what you learned. The order matters because it helps the listener follow your story from start to end. Most of your answer should be about the Action, because that is where the assessor sees the Behaviour. Keep the Situation and Task short. Write your answers in the past tense, because you are describing something that has already happened. It is a good habit to write a few STAR examples down before the application so that you are not trying to invent them under pressure. Practise saying them aloud and keep them to a sensible length. Each example should be real and something you can talk about in more detail if the interviewer asks.

questions.prompt: What does the S in STAR stand for?
questions.hint: S stands for Situation.

questions.prompt: In STAR, what does the letter T stand for?
questions.hint: T stands for Task.

questions.prompt: Which word completes STAR: Situation, Task, ___, Result?
questions.hint: A stands for Action.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four parts of STAR?
questions.hint: R stands for Result.

questions.prompt: In STAR, which part sets the scene briefly?
questions.hint: The Situation sets the scene.

questions.prompt: In STAR, which part says what you were responsible for or trying to achieve?
questions.hint: The Task explains your responsibility or aim.

questions.prompt: In STAR, which part describes what you personally did?
questions.hint: The Action is what you personally did.

questions.prompt: In STAR, which part says what happened and what you learned?
questions.hint: The Result is the outcome and the learning.

questions.prompt: Which part of a STAR answer should be the longest?
questions.hint: Most of the answer should be the Action.

questions.prompt: What is the STAR method used for?

options.text: Deciding which grade a role should be
Checking your reading speed in a test
Structuring an example in an application

questions.hint: STAR structures examples for Behaviours questions.

items.title: Level 1: STAR in practice: I, not we
items.body: A STAR answer works best when it follows a few simple habits. First, say I rather than we. The assessor is scoring you, not the group you were part of. If you say we organised an event, the assessor does not know what you did. Say 'I booked the hall, I wrote to the speakers and I counted the tickets'. Second, spend most of your answer on the Action. Describe your steps in the order you took them. Third, use real detail. Numbers, dates, names of places and the outcome all help. For example, 'I raised £450 for the school' is stronger than 'I raised some money'. Fourth, finish with a clear Result, and say what you learned, or what you would do differently. Fifth, be honest. Do not invent or exaggerate, because interviewers ask follow-up questions and will notice a story that does not hold together. A strong answer is specific and honest. A weak answer is vague, such as 'we organised an event and it went well', or it only describes the situation without saying what you did. Before you submit an application, read your examples again and check that the Action and Result are clear. Check the word limit and the question asked.

questions.prompt: In a STAR answer, which word should you use about your own actions?
questions.hint: Say I, because the assessor is scoring you.

questions.prompt: Why should you say I rather than we?

options.text: It is the usual style in official writing
It sounds more confident to the listener
It keeps the answer a little shorter
The assessor is scoring you, not the group

questions.hint: The assessor needs to know what you did.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives the strongest detail?

options.text: A lot of money was raised for the school
We raised quite a lot for the school
I raised £450 for the school in one afternoon
I raised a decent sum for the school

questions.hint: A specific figure makes the Result clear.

questions.prompt: Which part of the answer should take up most of your time?
questions.hint: Action is where the Behaviour is shown.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a weak STAR answer?

options.text: I booked the hall and sold 80 tickets
We organised an event and it went well
I counted the money and banked it
I wrote to six speakers and four agreed

questions.hint: The first is vague and uses we.

questions.prompt: What should you do with the Result?

options.text: Keep it vague if it did not go perfectly
Swap it for a longer description of the scene
Make it clear and say what you learned from it
Make it the longest part of the answer

questions.hint: A clear Result completes the story.

questions.prompt: In a STAR answer, what should you avoid?
questions.hint: Do not invent or exaggerate, because assessors ask follow-up questions.

questions.prompt: Why are interviewers likely to ask follow-up questions?

options.text: To see whether you get flustered
To fill up the time in the interview
To check that the example is true
To teach you how to use STAR

questions.hint: Follow-up questions check that the story is real.

questions.prompt: What type of answer does the passage describe as strong?
questions.hint: A strong answer is specific and honest.

questions.prompt: Before submitting an application, what should you check?

options.text: That you included everything you have done
That you used the longest words
That the Action and Result are clear

questions.hint: Check the Action and Result are clear.

items.title: Level 1: Home and unpaid experience, the basics
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: You may have learned important skills outside paid work. Running a household, caring for children or relatives, volunteering, helping at a school, serving on a committee, organising a community event and managing a family budget all build skills the Civil Service values. These include planning, organising, communicating, solving problems, handling money, keeping records and supporting others under pressure. Many people who have not had a paid job, or who have had a break from work, worry that they have nothing to offer. This is not true. The Experience and Behaviours elements are about what you have done, not whether you were paid. In an application you should describe unpaid experience in the language of work. For example, say 'I managed the household budget of £2,000 a month' rather than 'I'm just a housewife'. Never apologise for your experience and never use the word just. Give real detail, such as how much money, how many people and how often. Explain the result of what you did. Be honest, because assessors may ask follow-up questions, and do not exaggerate. Choose examples that match what the advert asks for, so that the assessor can see the link. If you are unsure whether something counts, the answer is usually that it does.

questions.prompt: Caring for a relative counts as which kind of activity?

options.text: Paid work done for an agency
A hobby with no link to work skills
An activity too informal to count

questions.hint: Caring is unpaid but builds real skills.

questions.prompt: Managing a family budget builds which skill?
questions.hint: Budgeting builds the skill of handling money.

questions.prompt: Running a household helps you build which skill the Civil Service values?
questions.hint: Planning and organising are built by running a household.

questions.prompt: Which wording works best in an application?

options.text: I managed the household budget of £2,000 a month
I'm just a housewife, but I did look after the money
I did not really do anything formal at home
I only looked after the house and the children

questions.hint: It uses work language and a specific figure.

questions.prompt: Which word should you avoid when describing unpaid experience?
questions.hint: Avoid minimising words such as just.

questions.prompt: What do the Experience and Behaviours elements depend on?

options.text: What you have done, paid or unpaid
Whether you were paid for it
Whether the work was in government

questions.hint: They are about what you have done, not whether you were paid.

questions.prompt: A parent helps run a school fete. Which element can this activity be offered as evidence for?
questions.hint: Volunteering is unpaid but valid evidence.

questions.prompt: What should you add to an example from home life?

options.text: Real detail like amounts, people involved and the result
An apology explaining that it was only done at home, not paid
A promise that you will learn more about the job if hired
A comment on how hard it was to fit around other duties

questions.hint: Real detail makes the example convincing.

questions.prompt: Why should you not exaggerate unpaid experience?

options.text: It is against the law to have hobbies

questions.hint: Follow-up questions test that examples are true.

questions.prompt: If you are unsure whether something counts as evidence, what is usually true?
questions.hint: Most real activity counts if you can show the link.
